articles.title: Therapeutic targeting of cGAS-STING signaling in epithelial inflammation.
articles.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway is a central regulator of immune surveillance, linking infection, stress, and injury to inflammatory signaling. However, dysregulated pathway activation can drive unresolved inflammation and tissue damage, which is particularly relevant in the pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and cutaneous epithelia. Given the context-dependent effects of cGAS-STING activation, precisely modulating this pathway for therapeutic benefit while preserving its protective functions is a rapidly emerging area of research. In this review, we discuss cGAS-STING signaling in the epithelia and related pathological manifestations. Notably, we bridge key nodes underlying cGAS-STING-mediated inflammation with therapeutic strategies currently advancing through preclinical and clinical development, including small-molecule antagonists, pathway modulators, and proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC)-based degraders. Finally, we discuss tissue-directed therapeutic delivery and describe translational difficulties in clinical application.

articles.title: Immunoregulation by lysophosphatidylcholine: mechanisms, determinants, and therapeutics.
articles.abstract: Lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) is a bioactive lysophospholipid and circulating metabolite that is increasingly recognized as an important regulator of immune responses and tissue homeostasis. However, its immunoregulatory effects are diverse and sometimes opposing across cell types and disease contexts, and the factors underlying this variability remain to be examined. Advances in structural biology, lipidomics, and lipid metabolism provide new insights into how LPC's molecular structure, its interactions with membrane proteins, and its metabolic fate shape its biological effects and contribute to disease processes. In this article, we review the mechanisms by which LPC regulates membrane proteins, the factors determining its immunoregulatory effects, and therapeutic strategies targeting LPC and its metabolic pathways.

articles.title: Pharmacology of glycine-activated receptors.
articles.abstract: Glycine is widely recognized as an important neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS), primarily due to its well-established role in inhibitory neurotransmission. However, recent evidence has demonstrated that glycine can directly activate three structurally and functionally distinct classes of plasma membrane receptors: inhibitory pentameric glycine receptors (GlyRs), the recently deorphanized metabotropic glycine receptor GPR158 (mGlyR), and non-conventional NMDA-type excitatory receptors composed of GluN1 and GluN3 subunits (eGlyRs). These discoveries have substantially broadened the concept of glycinergic signaling and revealed a diverse repertoire of mechanisms through which glycine regulates neuronal function. In this review, we provide an integrated overview of the pharmacology of the three classes of glycine-activated receptors, with particular emphasis on small-molecule ligands, their mechanisms of action, and their associated binding sites. While substantial progress has led to the identification of several orthosteric ligands and allosteric modulators targeting inhibitory and excitatory GlyRs, the pharmacology of glycine-activated receptors is still relatively limited, particularly that of the metabotropic glycine receptor GPR158. Critical gaps remain to be addressed through the development of additional modulatory molecules with greater receptor specificity and subunit selectivity. In addition, the physiological consequences of simultaneously regulating multiple glycine-sensitive systems, including membrane receptors and glycine transporters, remains unclear. Further advances are expected to accelerate the discovery of selective ligands for glycine-activated receptors, providing valuable experimental tools to dissect the complexity of glycinergic signaling in the CNS. These discoveries may also contribute to establishing glycinergic receptors as promising therapeutic targets for a broad range of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.

articles.title: Click and bioorthogonal chemistry in drug delivery and bioconjugation: Design principles, biological performance, and translational outlook.
articles.abstract: The development of click chemistry has transformed the design and construction of modern drug delivery systems by providing robust, highly selective, and efficient chemical strategies for constructing complex and well-defined therapeutic platforms. What began as a synthetic methodology for reliable molecular ligation has evolved into a cornerstone of precision nanomedicine, enabling covalent bond formation in complex biological environments without disrupting native cellular processes. By simplifying molecular assembly into modular and broadly accessible reactions, click chemistry has expanded the ability of researchers to design sophisticated bioconjugates and multifunctional nanoparticles without relying on technically demanding synthetic routes. These advances have profoundly influenced the development of targeted therapeutics, molecular imaging, theranostics, and precision medicine by facilitating the controlled integration of drugs, targeting ligands, imaging probes, and stimuli-responsive functionalities into a wide range of delivery systems. This review examines the major reaction classes that define this evolution, with emphasis on copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition, and inverse-electron-demand Diels-Alder chemistry, while also considering context-dependent approaches such as thiol-based conjugation, carbonyl coupling, sulfur fluoride exchange, and photoclick chemistry. Rather than treating these reactions as interchangeable tools, this review uses a context-dependent framework to connect reaction kinetics, reactive-handle and catalyst burden, product stability, chemoselectivity, and biological compatibility with drug-delivery performance and translational feasibility. This perspective spans controlled synthesis, ex vivo bioconjugation, ligation in biological media and living systems, in vivo pretargeting, and post-localization activation, allowing reaction choice to be evaluated according to the biological and operational demands of the intended application. By integrating chemical design with biological performance and translational considerations across multiple delivery and bioconjugation platforms, this review provides an application-oriented framework for selecting click reactions according to where and how bond formation must occur.

articles.title: Cell-encapsulating polymeric microgels based on droplet microfluidic technology: material design, crosslinking strategies, and biomedical applications.
articles.abstract: Cell-encapsulating microgels are indispensable platforms across biomedical disciplines, offering tunable three-dimensional (3D) microenvironments, physical protection, and efficient mass transport for living cells. Although droplet microfluidics provides unprecedented control over microgel fabrication, microgel performance is intrinsically dictated by crosslinking kinetics and mechanics. Shifting away from conventional, fragmented taxonomies of microfluidic devices, materials, and chemistries, this review offers an integrated, crosslinking-centered paradigm. We systematically examine how droplet-scale processing coupled with crosslinking dynamics governs network properties, cell fate, and functional performance. By dissecting the critical trade-offs between rapid gelation, cytocompatibility, transport phenomena, structural stability, and bio-degradation, this review establishes an application-driven framework to guide the rational design and translation of next-generation cell-laden microgels.

articles.title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.

articles.title: Natural products as modulators of Hippo signaling: mechanisms, pharmacology and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Hippo signaling pathway regulates tissue homeostasis and contributes to cancer, inflammatory disorders, metabolic diseases, neurological diseases, and tissue degeneration. Although synthetic Hippo-targeted agents show therapeutic potential, resistance and safety concerns limit their application. Natural products have emerged as promising modulators but their mechanisms remain incompletely integrated. PURPOSE: This article summarizes how natural products regulate Hippo signaling, focusing on molecular targets, regulatory networks, disease-specific effects, and the complementary characteristics of natural products and synthetic Hippo-targeted agents. METHODS: Records were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection by searching with "Hippo" and terms related to natural compounds (phytochemicals, natural compounds, natural products, herbal, botanical, TCM) as keywords, restricted to Articles. RESULTS: Natural products modulate Hippo signaling through direct interactions and network regulation. In cancer, they commonly activate Hippo signaling by promoting YAP/TAZ phosphorylation, cytoplasmic retention, or degradation, thereby inhibiting tumor progression and resistance. In non-malignant diseases, they restore tissue homeostasis by regulating pathological Hippo activity. Compared with synthetic agents, natural products provide multitarget network regulation and lower baseline toxicity, whereas synthetic compounds offer higher target specificity and more predictable pharmacokinetics. However, limited target validation, incomplete pharmacokinetic and ADME characterization, inadequate long-term safety assessment, and the paucity of clinical evidence continue to impede the clinical translation of natural products. CONCLUSION: Natural products act as context-dependent Hippo modulators and represent promising candidates for Hippo-targeted therapy. Pleiotropic properties and complementary advantages with synthetic drugs can provide new strategies for precision intervention. Future studies require rigorous validation and clinical investigation to support their translation.

articles.title: Immunopathological mechanisms linking atherosclerosis and ischemic stroke: From microenvironmental vulnerability to precision therapeutics.
articles.abstract: Atherosclerotic ischemic stroke results from a multistage process in which systemic susceptibility and local arterial biology converge to generate plaque vulnerability, thrombosis, embolization, and cerebral ischemia. This review critically integrates experimental, human tissue, observational, imaging, and randomized clinical evidence across this continuum. We distinguish disturbed flow-induced endothelial dysfunction and intimal retention of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins as upstream processes from macrophage dysfunction, defective efferocytosis, vascular smooth muscle cell remodeling, pathological neovascularization, and intraplaque hemorrhage that promote structural vulnerability. We then examine how plaque rupture and, with less direct cerebrovascular evidence, superficial erosion interact with platelet activation, coagulation, and neutrophil-associated immunothrombosis to produce artery-to-artery embolization or hemodynamic ischemia. Systemic modifiers, including clonal hematopoiesis, trained immunity, gut-derived metabolites, psychological stress, infection, and environmental exposures, are evaluated according to evidence maturity and stroke-specific relevance. Poststroke neuroimmune-hematopoietic reprogramming is considered an experimentally supported but incompletely validated feedback mechanism in humans. Among imaging-defined plaque features, carotid intraplaque hemorrhage has comparatively mature human prognostic evidence, whereas many molecular signatures remain investigational. Emerging single-cell, spatial, multiomic, molecular-imaging, and thrombus-profiling technologies are considered separately from clinically validated risk tools. Finally, therapeutic strategies are organized by mechanism and strength of clinical evidence, distinguishing established lipid-lowering, antithrombotic, and reperfusion approaches from investigational inflammatory, lipoprotein(a)-directed, and genome-editing strategies. This evidence-based framework identifies where mechanistic insight is mature, where translation remains uncertain, and how precision prevention may be advanced in atherosclerotic stroke. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Atherosclerotic ischemic stroke is driven by more than arterial narrowing: plaque vulnerability, immune inflammation, thrombosis, and impaired cerebral perfusion interact to determine clinical risk. By separating findings supported by human cerebrovascular evidence from emerging experimental mechanisms, this review clarifies opportunities and limitations for improved risk stratification, biomarker development, and mechanism-guided prevention.

articles.title: A Nucleolus-Penetrating Peptide Platform Enables DDX24 PET Imaging and Targeted Degradation Therapy for Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer.
articles.abstract: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), particularly the prevalent PSMA-negative subtype, lacks effective imaging-guided therapy options. Here, we report a nucleolus-penetrating peptide platform targeting DDX24, an oncogenic RNA helicase overexpressed in CRPC. Using bacterial surface display with iterative MACS/FACS screening, a leading DDX24-binding peptide (TDP-2, Kd = 17.63 ± 7.72μM) is identified. This single peptide is engineered into two imaging-guided therapy modalities: (1) a 64Cu-labeled PET probe ([64Cu]Cu-DOTA-TDP-2, >99% radiochemical purity) enabling specific, non-invasive imaging of DDX24-positive CRPC tumors in vivo (SUVmean 0.55 ± 0.08, T/M ratio 6.59 ± 0.71); and (2) a peptide-based PROTAC (TDP-2-PROTAC) that recruits the VHL E3 ligase to induce targeted, proteasome-dependent degradation of DDX24 (DC50 =49.1μM). TDP-2-PROTAC selectively suppresses CRPC cell proliferation (PC-3, DU145) while sparing non-malignant cells, and significantly inhibits tumor growth in xenograft models, accompanied by a reduction in tumoral [18F]FDG uptake and influx ([18F]FDG PET: SUV 1.29 ±0.45 vs 2.48 ± 0.24 in controls, p < 0.001). This integrated platform establishes DDX24 as a viable target for PSMA-negative CRPC and demonstrates the power of peptide-based tools for accessing intracellular oncogenic drivers.

articles.title: An X-encoded pyrimidinergic checkpoint: P2Y4 controls TLR7-IFN-α response in human plasmacytoid dendritic cells.
articles.abstract: Pyrimidinergic molecules such as UTP are released upon cell death and act as damage-associated molecular patterns by activating P2Y receptors, thereby shaping innate immune responses. P2Y receptors have recently been attracting attention as potential therapeutic targets to combat infectious, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases which are increasingly being discovered to affect men and women differently. While sex differences in antiviral immunity have been extensively linked to enhanced IFN-I production in females, sex-specific anti-inflammatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the UTP-responsive, X-chromosomally encoded P2RY4 to be significantly more highly expressed in female pDCs. Single-cell gene expression analysis revealed a female-specific correlation between P2RY4 and Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) expression. Functional interrogation of this axis provided novel insights into the role of P2Y4 in regulating various cytokines and chemokines, calcium signalling and interferon regulatory factor (IRF) expression. Our findings uncover the nuanced sex differences in P2Y4 function and propose pyrimidinergic signalling as an overlooked modulator of pDC immunity.

articles.title: Lipid nanoparticles supplemented with oligocationic lipids and pH-releasable PEG show enhanced siRNA delivery.
articles.abstract: The composition of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) strongly affects the nucleic acid loading, the interactions with biological targets, the effective endosomal escape, and the cytosolic release at the target site. To integrate these requirements and evaluate the effect of excipients commonly used in LNP production, we comparatively screened a set of LNP formulations containing nucleic acid condensing tetraArginine-[G2]-distearoyl glycerol (OCE), and different fusogenic/ionizable commercial lipids: DOPE, DODAP, D-Lin-MC3-DMA, ALC-0315, and SM-102. Three PEGylated agents were investigated to evaluate their effect on colloidal stability and transfection performance: pH-sheddable DSPE-hydrazone-PEG2kDa (DSPE-Hz-PEG), diffusible DMG-PEG2kDa (DMG-PEG) and non-releasable DSPE-PEG2kDa (NR-DSPE-PEG). The combination of OCE with the commercial lipids yielded LNPs with ~100 nm sizes, and + 35/40 mV z-potentials, and high siRNA loading efficiencies (~90%), nearly doubling those of OCE-free formulations. LNPs containing OCE and the ionizable lipids D-Lin-MC3-DMA, ALC-0315, and SM-102 yielded the highest gene silencing in eGFP-expressing H1299 cells, with IC₅₀ values between 0.32 and 0.47 nM. In contrast, all OCE-free formulations and formulations containing OCE in combination with DOPE or DODAP, yielded remarkably lower gene silencing. LNPs obtained with OCE and SM-102 coated with 3 and 5 mol% DSPE-Hz-PEG and NR-DSPE-PEG produced colloidally stable formulations also in presence of serum. The 5 mol% DSPE-Hz-PEG coating provided effective charge shielding at pH 7.4 while PEG detached under endosomal conditions (pH 5.5). This behavior enhanced cytosolic siRNA delivery, achieving an eGFP silencing IC₅₀ of 3.22 nM owing to efficient OCE-LNP endosomal escape enabled by spatially controlled, pH-triggered cleavage of the PEG-lipid. NR-DSPE-PEG showed reduced endosomal escape and transfection (IC₅₀: 82 nM) while DMG-PEG exhibited poor serum stability due to premature detachment, making it a less effective stealth agent.

articles.title: An injectable hydrogel loaded with selenium and copper for self-amplification of toxic reactive oxygen species in breast cancer therapy.
articles.abstract: A cascade toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) amplification system was developed for locoregional therapy of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Selenium (Se) (from sodium selenite (SS)) and copper (Cu) (from cupric sulfate (CS)) ions were coordinated with the catechol groups of hyaluronic acid-dopamine (HD) to achieve rheological tuning of a hydrogel structure. Because of enhanced viscoelasticity and shear-thinning behavior, the engineered HD/SS/CS hydrogel can be readily injected through a syringe needle, and its slow biodegradation and sustained release of therapeutic cargos reduce the necessary dosing frequency. Se ions increase H2O2 levels spontaneously in cancer cells, and Cu ions catalyze the conversion of H2O2 to OH radicals based on Fenton-like chemistry. Se promotes glutathione (GSH) depletion, increases toxic ROS production and lipid peroxidation, which ultimately triggers apoptosis. Cu also contributes to GSH oxidation, thereby enhancing apoptotic signaling, and induces cuproptosis through the downregulation of ferredoxin 1 and lipoic acid synthetase, as well as the aggregation of dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase. Through the concerted actions of these mineral ions, multiple programmed cell death pathways are activated, thus enabling an efficient and safe strategy for the treatment of localized TNBC.

articles.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts promote thyroid cancer progression and reduce radioiodide uptake via lactylation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Radioiodine (RAI) therapy is a cornerstone of thyroid cancer management, but impaired iodide uptake limits its efficacy. How distinct cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) populations alter tumor-cell iodide handling remains incompletely understood. We investigated a complement factor D-positive (CFD+) CAF population and the associated lactate-dependent paracrine signaling pathway. METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics sequencing (ST-seq) were used to characterize CAF heterogeneity. Histone H3 lysine 27 lactylation (H3K27la) CUT&Tag and ChIP-qPCR analyses were integrated with molecular and functional experiments. Thyroid cancer cells were evaluated in CAF co-culture systems, and xenografts were used to examine tumor growth and NIS expression. Cellular radioiodide-handling capacity was assessed by a sodium/iodide symporter (NIS)-inhibitable 125 I uptake assay. RESULTS: CFD + CAF exhibited enhanced glycolytic activity and lactate production, accompanied by increased AARS1-associated H3K27la. H3K27la enrichment at PDGFA and PDGFB regulatory regions was associated with increased expression of these ligands. CAF-tumor-cell signaling implicated the PDGF/PDGFR-RAS/MAPK pathway in NIS downregulation and reduced iodide uptake. Sorafenib attenuated tumor growth and was associated with increased NIS expression and cellular 125 I uptake. CONCLUSION: A lactate-AARS1-H3K27la-PDGF signaling program in CFD + CAFs is associated with thyroid cancer progression and impaired NIS-dependent iodide uptake. These data support investigation of stromal PDGF signaling and sorafenib-mediated redifferentiation strategies; restoration of in vivo RAI treatment sensitivity remains to be demonstrated.

articles.title: Cytotoxicity-driven prediction of developmental toxicity is complemented by transcriptional biomarker signatures of perturbed neuroectodermal differentiation in vitro.
articles.abstract: Developmental toxicity testing requires human-relevant approaches that provide both predictive information and mechanistic insight. Here, we investigated the relative contributions of cytotoxicity and targeted transcriptomics to developmental toxicity assessment in a human induced pluripotent stem cell-based model of early neuroectodermal differentiation. A biologically anchored 190-gene transcript biomarker panel was derived from a previously published transcriptome dataset using complementary biomarker-selection strategies. An independent set of 18 developmental toxicants and non-toxicants was then evaluated based on concentration-dependent cytotoxicity normalized to maternal plasma Cmax values and biomarker expression. We found that cytotoxicity provided substantial discriminatory power in random forest-based classification of developmental toxicants and non-toxicants, yielding an AUC of 0.852, demonstrating robust discrimination for a complex and heterogeneous toxicological endpoint. In contrast, transcriptional responses were frequently detected at concentrations substantially below those causing cytotoxicity, but this increased sensitivity did not improve random forest classification of the two groups. Instead, targeted transcriptional profiling revealed compound-specific perturbation patterns that were not captured by cytotoxicity. Principal component analysis and Differentiation Pattern Clustering (DiPaC) distinguished impaired progression towards neuroectodermal identity from activation of divergent developmental transcriptional programs, exemplified by methoxyacetic acid and dimethadione, respectively. These findings demonstrate that cytotoxicity assessment normalized to physiological maternal plasma concentrations can provide substantial discriminatory information in an in vitro model of early embryonic development, while targeted transcriptional profiling provides complementary mechanistic insight into how developmental differentiation is perturbed. Distinguishing predictive from mechanistic value may therefore be important for the interpretation and integration of transcriptomic endpoints in developmental toxicity assessment.

articles.title: Redox-active copper nanoparticles attenuate colistin-induced nephrotoxicity by restoring Akt/GSK3β/mTOR-TFEB signaling and autophagic homeostasis in HK-2 cells and mice.
articles.abstract: Colistin is an indispensable last-line antibiotic against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, but its use is limited by dose-dependent acute kidney injury (AKI) with proximal tubular damage. Although oxidative stress is implicated, how it translates into tubular injury remains poorly defined, and antioxidant therapy alone shows limited efficacy. We investigated whether ultrasmall copper nanoparticles (Cu NPs), which approach the glomerular filtration threshold and accumulate in renal tubules, protect against colistin nephrotoxicity, using human proximal tubular epithelial HK-2 cells (colistin 200 µg/mL; Cu NPs 200 ng/mL) and female C57BL/6 mice (colistin 30 mg/kg/day; Cu NPs 250 µg/kg twice weekly). In HK-2 cells, colistin induced apoptosis, excess cytosolic and mitochondrial superoxide, mitochondrial fission, and dysregulated autophagy with LC3B accumulation and impaired flux, alongside Akt/GSK3β and mTOR suppression and excessive nuclear TFEB translocation. Pharmacological TFEB activation aggravated injury, indicating that maladaptive autophagy contributes to tubular death. Cu NPs scavenged these oxidants, reactivated Akt/GSK3β/mTOR signaling, and restored productive autophagic flux without suppressing nuclear TFEB, reducing apoptosis and preserving mitochondrial integrity, whereas N-acetylcysteine failed to reproduce these signaling effects. Autophagic flux, rather than the absolute level of nuclear TFEB, therefore determined tubular outcome. Cu NPs accumulated preferentially in the kidney and were protective at sub-toxic doses; in vivo, they attenuated tubular injury and apoptosis and modulated autophagy-related signaling, although functional renal improvement was not demonstrated. Thus, Cu NPs attenuate colistin-induced tubular injury by modulating the Akt/GSK3β/mTOR-TFEB axis and restoring autophagic homeostasis rather than acting solely as antioxidants, supporting their potential as a nephroprotective strategy.

articles.title: Single-cell and spatial omics in urologic cancer immunotherapy: bibliometric and registry mapping with an exploratory full-text assessment.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Single-cell and spatial omics can inform research on immunotherapy response and resistance. We mapped publication activity and ClinicalTrials.gov study designs and explored evidence types in a targeted full-text subset of urologic cancer studies. METHODS: Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus records published in 2008-2025 were locked on 13 July 2026. Revision-stage eligibility reconciliation retained 538 records; 466 native Web of Science records supplied temporal-analysis inputs. A targeted full-text assessment was supplemented by a random audit of 100 previously non-selected records and independent reassessment of 40 selected studies. Evidence classes included treatment-exposed human data, association replication, computational proxies, experimental mechanisms, and prognosis. ClinicalTrials.gov records were analyzed separately. RESULTS: The 538-record corpus included 440 publications from 2023-2025 (81.8%). The targeted assessment included 122 original studies among 135 assessed reports. In the random audit, 15/100 records were C1 or C2b: three C1 and 12 C2b. One C1 report contained cell-level descriptive evidence without a patient-level marker-outcome analysis. The initial evidence-class agreement was 92/100 (Cohen's kappa, 0.890) in this audit and 31/40 (kappa, 0.682) in the selected-study reassessment. Public-cohort reuse and exploratory analyses limited clinical interpretation. Of 10 ClinicalTrials.gov records, one had a verified reported omics component, eight documented planned or ongoing components, and one was withdrawn without accrual. CONCLUSION: Bibliometric activity increased in the retained corpus. The random audit identified treatment-related reports missed by targeted retrieval, limiting claims about evidence completeness. Cell-level descriptions, patient-level associations, and locked-model validation require separate interpretation. Neither selected-study proportions nor bibliometric attention establishes field-wide clinical maturity. Registry plans require component-specific verification of implementation and reporting.

articles.title: Pathological complete response and major pathological response as surrogate endpoints for recurrence-free survival in perioperative immunotherapy for hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: High post-resection recurrence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) limits long-term survival. Perioperative immunotherapy, including neoadjuvant therapy for resectable HCC and conversion therapy for unresectable HCC, has become a research hotspot. Whether pathological complete response (pCR) and major pathological response (MPR) can serve as surrogate endpoints for recurrence-free survival (RFS) remains unclear, with important implications for accelerating trial design. OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the correlation between pCR/MPR and RFS following HCC perioperative immunotherapy, quantitatively synthesize hazard ratios (HRs) of pCR/MPR versus non-pCR/non-MPR for RFS (and overall survival, OS) across studies, and assess their reliability as surrogate endpoints. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) and Wanfang Data databases (from inception to June 2026), supplemented by manual searching and citation tracking. The DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model was used to pool effect sizes. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistic and Q test. Sensitivity analysis was performed using leave-one-out method. Subgroup analyses were conducted by treatment stage (neoadjuvant vs. conversion), treatment regimen (ICI mono/dual vs. ICI + TKI vs. triple therapy), study design (prospective vs. retrospective), and MPR definition (≥70% vs. ≥ 90% necrosis). Publication bias was evaluated using Egger's regression test. RESULTS: The systematic review included 21 studies for descriptive analysis. The meta-analysis included 10 studies reporting HR values: 5 pCR studies (n = 720) and 6 MPR studies (n = 785), one of which (NeoHCC, D'Alessio 2024) (D'Alessio et al., Lancet Oncol, 2024, 25(12), 1465-1475) encompassed both. The pCR vs. non-pCR → RFS/DFS: Pooled HR = 0.342 (95% CI: 0.248-0.472), p < 0.000001, heterogeneity I2 = 0.0%. In sensitivity analysis, pooled HR remained stable at 0.244-0.354. MPR vs. non-MPR → RFS/PFS: Pooled HR = 0.291 (95% CI: 0.155-0.548), p = 0.000132, I2 = 66.6%. Heterogeneity was primarily driven by one study containing non-immunotherapy cohorts (Zhang 2024, n = 481) (Zhang et al., Hepatobiliary Pancreat Dis Int, 2025, 24(2), 157-163); after exclusion, I2 decreased to 0.0%, HR = 0.215. CONCLUSION: The pCR and MPR after perioperative immunotherapy are strongly associated with improved RFS in HCC, corresponding to approximately 66% and 70% reductions in recurrence risk, respectively. These findings support pCR/MPR as promising surrogate endpoints, although prospective randomized validation remains necessary.

articles.title: Effectiveness and safety of different administration routes of medical cannabis or cannabinoids for chronic pain in adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis with GRADE assessment.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic pain lasting more than 3 months affects more than one billion people globally, ranking as the third most prevalent health burden, after cardiovascular diseases and malignancies. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of medical cannabis or cannabinoids for chronic pain in adults, with prespecified subgroup analyses stratified by pain etiology and administration route to support precision pain management. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library from each database's inception to 15 March 2025. The certainty of evidence was assessed with the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. The focused outcomes were pain relief, sleep quality, physical and emotional functioning, anxiety, depression, and adverse events. RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were involved. Compared to placebo, palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) (SMD = -0.82, 95% CI:-1.36 to -0.29; very low) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) (SMD = -0.41, 95% CI:-0.74 to -0.07; low) provided pain relief, and a THC/cannabidiol (CBD) combination significantly improved sleep quality (SMD = -0.43, 95% CI:-0.62 to -0.24; moderate). Regarding safety outcomes, compared to placebo, THC (RR = 3.55, 95% CI: 2.21 to 5.68; low) and THC/CBD (RR = 2.70, 95% CI: 1.60 to 4.53; high) had a relatively high rate of dizziness, and THC (RR = 2.72, 95% CI: 1.76 to 4.22; low) and THC/CBD (RR = 2.92, 95% CI: 1.74 to 4.90; high) had a significant risk of somnolence. THC/CBD elevated nausea risk (RR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.26 to 2.60; high), while THC increased dry mouth incidence (RR = 3.14, 95% CI: 1.75 to 5.63; moderate). Additionally, compared with placebo for pain relief, CBD demonstrated the greatest effectiveness for cancer-related pain (SMD = -1.62, 95% CI:-2.03 to -1.21), whereas PEA showed optimal effectiveness in non-cancer-related pain (SMD = -0.82, 95% CI:-1.31 to -0.33). CONCLUSION: This study suggested that medical cannabis or cannabinoids might have certain efficacy for adult chronic pain. PEA and THC provided pain relief, while the THC/CBD combination showed a potential benefit for sleep quality improvement. THC was associated with increased risks of dizziness, somnolence, and dry mouth, and THC/CBD was associated with dizziness, somnolence, and nausea. Subgroup analyses suggested that treatment response might vary by pain etiology and administration route. Given that the evidence certainty is mainly low to very low, the research conclusion still requires a large sample and high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to be verified. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://osf.io/h56g9, Unique Identifier: 10.17605/OSF.IO/H56G9.

articles.title: Model-informed characterisation of the target therapeutic window for dexamethasone by quantitatively balancing foetal lung maturation and neurotoxicity in pregnant rats.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Dexamethasone, a first-line treatment for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS), promotes foetal lung maturation whilst simultaneously inducing neurotoxicity in offspring. We aimed to define the therapeutic window of dexamethasone for the treatment of NRDS. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Pregnant rats were given dexamethasone at 0.1 or 0.4 mg·kg-1 to simulate clinically equivalent prenatal dexamethasone exposure. Half of the rats were anaesthetised, and surfactant proteins A and B in foetal lungs quantified. A pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) model was developed to determine the minimum effective concentration. The remaining rats, delivered naturally, and their offspring underwent open-field testing. Messenger RNA sequencing of the foetal hippocampus was performed, and concentration-toxicity assays were conducted using H19-7/IGF-IR cells. Data were integrated with a maternal-foetal physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to determine the maximum tolerated concentration. A clinical PBPK for dexamethasone in pregnant women was used to simulate a potentially optimal dosing regimen. KEY RESULTS: The PK/PD model adequately characterised dexamethasone-induced foetal lung maturation and indicated a minimal effective concentration of 1.63 ng·ml-1. The offspring of PDE rats exhibited significant behavioural changes. mRNA sequencing analysis suggested that neurotoxicity was mediated via the Wnt pathway and renin-angiotensin system, with BDNF and CMA1 identified as potential biomarkers of neurotoxicity. Cell-based assays suggested a neurotoxic threshold concentration of 17 ng·ml-1. For a therapeutic window of 1.63-17 ng·ml-1, PBPK model simulations indicated that a reduced dose regimen of 2.5 or 3 mg every 8 h for six doses may represent an optimised therapeutic strategy. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: This model-informed precision dosing strategy provides a rational approach to optimising clinical dexamethasone dosing regimens.

articles.title: Effects of an optimized beta-glucan-based formulation on symptoms, functional capacity, and systemic inflammation in patients with COPD: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by persistent airflow limitation, chronic inflammation, and oxidative stress, leading to progressive functional impairment and reduced quality of life. Beta-glucan possesses immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties, but its therapeutic potential in COPD remains poorly defined. This study aimed to optimize a combined formulation of beta-glucan, broccoli extract, and quercetin (Pro β-Glucan+) through in vitro evaluation and to investigate its clinical efficacy in patients with stable COPD. METHODS: HFL1 lung fibroblasts were treated with different ratios of Pro β-Glucan+®, and cell viability and wound healing assays were performed to identify the optimal formulation. The selected ratio was evaluated in a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. A total of 42 participants were randomized, of whom 38 completed the study and were included in the final analysis (Pro β-Glucan+, n = 19; placebo, n = 19). Prespecified primary outcome was FEV1. Secondary outcomes included clinical symptoms, functional capacity, health status, inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers, and patient satisfaction. RESULTS: The 10:3:2 ratio (beta-glucan:broccoli extract:quercetin) significantly enhanced HFL1 cell cell viability and wound healing activity among the tested formulations and was selected for clinical evaluation. Pro β-Glucan+® was well tolerated and associated with within-group improvements in dyspnea, respiratory symptoms, functional capacity, and health status after 12 weeks, with significant between-group differences in mMRC and CAT scores at week 12. No significant within- or between-group difference was observed in the prespecified primary outcome, FEV1, or in systemic inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers. Patient satisfaction was higher with Pro β-Glucan+® than with placebo. CONCLUSION: The optimized Pro β-Glucan+® formulation demonstrated in vitro biological activity and was associated with improvements in several clinical outcomes in patients with stable COPD. Significant between-group differences were observed in mMRC and CAT scores at week 12. These findings support further investigation of this combination as an adjunctive nutritional intervention for COPD management. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05878834, identifier NCT05878834.

articles.title: Dissolving and hydrogel-based polymeric microneedles for bacterial keratitis: materials, therapeutic payloads, design-performance relationships, and future perspectives.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Bacterial keratitis (BK) is a major cause of corneal visual impairment. Although topical antibiotics remain the mainstay of treatment, tear turnover, blinking, nasolacrimal drainage, and the corneal epithelial barrier limit drug residence and penetration. Polymeric microneedles, particularly dissolving and hydrogel-based systems, may enhance ocular residence of therapeutic agents and enable controlled or sustained drug release. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes corneal anatomy and ocular drug-delivery barriers, outlines the pathophysiology of bacterial keratitis, and evaluates microneedle platforms developed for ocular applications, with emphasis on dissolving and hydrogel-based polymeric systems for bacterial keratitis. A focused search of PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect was undertaken, supplemented by a search of Google Scholar to identify additional relevant studies. Relevant studies were compared according to polymer composition, microneedle dimensions and density, penetration depth, dissolution or swelling, and release kinetics. Polymer design-property relationships, including the effects of concentration, molecular weight, crosslinking, biodegradability, and post-administration polymer fate, are also discussed. EXPERT OPINION: Polymeric microneedles offer a promising strategy for overcoming corneal delivery barriers, but clinical translation will depend on reproducible manufacturing, mechanical and ocular safety, sterilization and storage stability, user-friendly application, and robust clinical evidence demonstrating advantages over optimized topical therapies.

articles.title: A bibliometric analysis of bibliometric research in pharmacology.
articles.abstract: Bibliometric papers are among the fastest-growing article types in pharmacology, yet the genre itself has seldom been examined with its own tools. We retrieved all Scopus records in the Pharmacology, Toxicology and Pharmaceutics subject area that mentioned 'bibliometric' or 'scientometric' in the title, abstract or keywords (n = 1979; search date 27 October 2026). After a five-step screening procedure that removed errata, duplicate versions and records outside the biomedical and pharmaceutical domain, 1823 documents were analysed. Output grew by 24.5% per year between 2006 and 2025 (doubling time 3.2 years). China-affiliated authors contributed 54.1% of documents but co-authored internationally on only 10.3% of them. Titles framed around 'hotspots', 'frontiers' or 'trends' rose from 9.1% of documents published up to 2020 to 34.4% of those published in 2023-2025, and a formulaic hotspot-plus-mapping title accounted for 29.8% of recent output. Production was concentrated in seven core journals, led by Frontiers in Pharmacology. In a negative binomial model of 913 articles and reviews (2015-2024), review status (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 2.01), international co-authorship (1.64) and acknowledged funding (1.38) were associated with higher citation counts and Chinese language publication with lower counts (0.16). The crude open access advantage (IRR 1.37) disappeared after adjustment for language, and template titles showed no independent association. The model explained only a small share of citation variance, and the associations are observational. The recent expansion of the genre reflects volume more than distinctive impact, which supports asking bibliometric submissions for a pharmacological question, transparent reporting and interpretation beyond descriptive mapping.

articles.title: An overlooked Gα subunit in cancer: GNA14-driven signaling rewires tumor growth and angiogenesis.
articles.abstract: GNA14, a key member of the Gαq/11 subfamily, functions as a G-protein α-subunit involved in diverse cellular signaling processes. Its expression is primarily regulated by genetic mutations and promoter methylation. Recent studies have demonstrated that GNA14 is aberrantly expressed in a wide range of tumor types, including vascular tumors, hepatocellular carcinoma, and endometrial carcinoma. By modulating key signaling pathways such as MAPK/JNK, Notch1/RB, and NF-κB, GNA14 plays a crucial role in regulating tumor cell proliferation, apoptosis, invasion, metastasis, and angiogenesis. By integrating and analyzing current research, this article provides a systematic overview of the molecular structure and functions of GNA14, as well as its expression patterns and mechanistic roles in vascular tumors and various cancers. It further explores the potential of GNA14 as a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target, offering new theoretical foundations and research perspectives for early tumor detection, precision therapy, and prognostic assessment.

articles.title: Endothelial cell-targeted nanotherapies for pulmonary vascular diseases.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary vascular endothelial cell (EC) dysfunction drives various pulmonary vascular diseases (PVD). Conventional pharmacological treatments often lack specificity. Current gene therapies rely on viral vectors, which often pose a safety concern. To address these issues, there is a critical need for delivery systems that can specifically target the pulmonary endothelium to ensure safety and therapeutic efficacy. AREAS COVERED: This review covers the fundamental principles of designing nanoparticles (NPs) for endothelial targeting, focusing on overcoming biological barriers, the impact of NP physicochemical properties on organ selectivity and NP-EC interactions, and active targeting strategies using specific ligands for receptor-mediated targeting. We also discuss the challenges and future perspectives of translating NP technologies to patient care. Literature published between 2007 and 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Google Scholar, and Web of Science databases. EXPERT OPINION: Precision lung-directed therapies for PVD require overcoming complex biological barriers through a deeper understanding of NP interactions with different cells and organs. This involves optimizing fundamental physicochemical properties of NPs to ensure pulmonary accumulation while utilizing specific ligands to enhance cellular uptake. Achieving clinical translation requires comprehensive safety assessments, manufacturing scalability, and standardized regulatory pathways. New technologies offer promising tools for developing personalized pulmonary nanomedicines.

articles.title: Practical considerations for the safe use of pembrolizumab or durvalumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin in advanced biliary tract Cancer.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pembrolizumab or durvalumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin is a first-line option for unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer. KEYNOTE-966 and TOPAZ-1 demonstrated improved overall survival, with similar rates of severe treatment-related adverse events compared with chemotherapy alone. However, biliary obstruction, cholangitis, stents, hepatic and renal dysfunction, frailty and polypharmacy complicate treatment delivery and adverse-event attribution. Distinguishing treatment toxicity from disease-related complications is therefore important when assessing clinical deterioration and making decisions about treatment interruption or resumption. AREAS COVERED: This narrative review examines drug-specific and overlapping toxicities, organ-system adverse events, drug-drug interactions, supportive medications, special populations, biliary stent management and pharmacovigilance needs. Treatment interruption, chemotherapy dose modification and diagnostic uncertainty are also discussed. Evidence was identified through PubMed and Embase searches covering January 2010 to September 2026. EXPERT OPINION: Available evidence does not establish a safety advantage for either checkpoint inhibitor. The opportunity to continue gemcitabine beyond eight cycles in KEYNOTE-966 makes cumulative chemotherapy exposure a practical consideration, but does not prove greater toxicity caused by pembrolizumab. Management depends on identifying the likely cause and deciding whether biliary intervention, corticosteroids or chemotherapy dose adjustment is appropriate. Evidence remains limited for patients with persistent cholestasis, poor performance status or frailty.

articles.title: Enhancing amorphous solid dispersions with alternative excipients: advances in drug formulation, drug-excipient insights, and regulatory landscape.
articles.abstract: Poor aqueous solubility remains a major cause of attrition in oral drug development, with amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) representing one of the most established enabling technologies to overcome this challenge. However, increasingly complex drugs candidates and demands for higher drug loads are stretching the boundaries of current excipient portfolios, driving interest in alternative carrier classes. Accordingly, this review critically examines the use of naturally derived alternative carriers, focusing on polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins in oral ASDs through a systematic literature analysis (2015-2026) comprising 41 excipients and 342 binary solid dispersions. Excipient families were compared in terms of drug loading, amorphization success, drug-excipient interactions, manufacturability, and regulatory considerations. Protein-based carriers spanned the broadest range of APIs, drug loads, and scalable manufacturing conditions, while consistently exhibiting the highest amorphization rates (∼79%), including weak acid, amphoteric, and weak base drugs, and stabilized amorphous APIs drug loads up to 90%. Lipid-based carriers also demonstrated high amorphization rates (∼76%), particularly with neutral compounds, while offering additional solubilization and permeability-enhancing capabilities. In contrast, polysaccharide-based systems revealed limited amorphization success associated with the employed processing techniques (∼35%). Furthermore, alternative excipients were shown to influence dissolution performance through mechanisms including reversible drug-protein interactions, colloidal lipidic species, and digestion-mediated transformations. Beyond direct formulation analysis, this review highlights the importance of regulatory qualification, material standardization, and harmonized performance evaluation methodologies as critical barriers to broader adoption. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of alternative carriers in expanding the excipient landscape, thus helping to support the next generation of ASD.

articles.title: Candidate molecular mechanisms of naproxen hepatotoxicity: an evidence-graded narrative review of bioactivation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and immune-mediated liver injury.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Naproxen sodium, a propionic acid-derived non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) introduced in 1976, has a favorable hepatic safety profile. Yet clinically apparent naproxen-induced liver injury (NILI) occurs rarely (~1-3 per 100,000 exposed patients), ranging from transient transaminase elevation to cholestatic hepatitis with ductopenia and, exceptionally, acute liver failure. Unlike diclofenac, naproxen lacks mechanistic synthesis. This review aimed to integrate and grade evidence for candidate mechanisms of naproxen hepatotoxicity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Molecular, biochemical, immunological, and clinical data were synthesized in a narrative review. Each candidate mechanism was graded using explicit criteria distinguishing naproxen-specific findings from mechanisms extrapolated from other NSAIDs or hepatotoxicants. KEY FINDINGS: Naproxen-specific evidence is strongest for hepatic bioactivation to a reactive acyl-β-D-glucuronide and a coenzyme-A thioester forming covalent protein adducts (isolated rat liver), ex vivo memory T-cell responses to an oxidative desmethyl-naproxen metabolite in a few patients, and rodent oxidative-stress and aminotransferase changes. Cyclooxygenase-dependent loss of hepatoprotection, mitochondrial permeability transition, ATP depletion, Keap1-Nrf2-ARE signaling, HLA-restricted sensitization, Kupffer-cell amplification, and BSEP/MRP2 interference are extrapolated or hypothetical for naproxen, and no study links these steps within one naproxen system. Convergence on intrinsic mitochondrial apoptosis is untested. Clinically, naproxen carries lower liver risk than diclofenac despite overlapping mechanistic potential. SIGNIFICANCE: This synthesis separates evidence-based from speculative mechanisms of naproxen hepatotoxicity, supporting causality assessment and prioritizing human-relevant experiments for mechanistic and pharmacovigilance research. Hepatoprotective and pharmacogenomic strategies are hypothesis-generating, not clinical recommendations. Only 4 of 12 graded nodes are naproxen-specific; the rest are hypotheses, not an established causal cascade.

articles.title: Targeting Integrin Signaling in Chronic Pain: From Extracellular Matrix Mechanotransduction to Neuroimmune Pharmacology.
articles.abstract: Chronic pain affects approximately one in five individuals worldwide and remains a major clinical challenge as existing analgesics often provide inadequate or short-term relief. Most conventional treatments primarily target neuronal excitability while the changes in the extracellular matrix (ECM) and surrounding cellular microenvironment that contribute to persistent pain remain largely overlooked. Growing evidence suggests that ECM remodelling and altered cell-matrix interactions contribute to pain sensitisation highlighting integrins as potential regulators of these processes. Integrins are heterodimeric transmembrane receptors that connect ECM proteins including collagen, laminin and fibronectin to the intracellular cytoskeleton and transmit mechanical and biochemical signals across the cell membrane. Through these interactions, integrins influence nociceptor sensitisation, schwann cell function, axonal plasticity, immune-cell activation and neuron-glia communication. This review examines the involvement of integrin signalling in different chronic pain conditions, focusing on how altered ECM-integrin interactions contribute to peripheral and central sensitisation. Particular attention is given to focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signalling, associated downstream pathways, mechanosensitive ion channels, and neuroimmune responses involved in persistent pain. We further discuss emerging therapeutic approaches including integrin-targeting monoclonal antibodies, RGD-based peptidomimetics, kinase inhibitors and nanotechnology-based drug-delivery systems. Although integrin-targeted therapies have been explored in cancer and inflammatory disorders yet their analgesic potential remains insufficiently investigated. Furthermore, the essential roles of integrins in neuronal survival, axonal regeneration and tissue repair raise concerns regarding the selectivity and safety of therapeutic inhibition. Understanding the contributions of individual integrin subtypes across different cell populations and pain conditions may help identify more precise therapeutic targets. Collectively this review also highlights the connection between ECM remodelling, integrin-mediated mechanotransduction, and neuroimmune signalling, providing a framework for developing mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for chronic pain.

articles.title: Small Molecule Inhibitors Targeting METTL3 in Cancer: Preclinical and Clinical Advances, Combination Strategies.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most prevalent epitranscriptomic modification in eukaryotic mRNA, precisely regulating RNA splicing, stability, and translation. Dysregulation of m6A is closely associated with tumorigenesis and therapeutic resistance. As the core catalytic component of the m6A methyltransferase complex, METTL3 is aberrantly expressed in various malignancies, particularly in non-small cell lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer, although its effects are highly context-dependent. AIM: This review summarizes the biological functions of METTL3 in solid tumors and the preclinical and clinical development of METTL3 small-molecule inhibitors. KEY FINDINGS: METTL3 regulates tumor progression and therapeutic resistance through m6A-dependent remodeling of oncogenic and immune transcripts. Small-molecule inhibitors, represented by STM2457 and its clinical derivative STC-15, show antitumor activity and can reverse drug resistance when combined with chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. Notably, METTL3 inhibition also mitigates chemotherapy-induced organ toxicity, suggesting a dual therapeutic benefit that may broaden the treatment window. CONCLUSION: METTL3 is a promising but context-dependent therapeutic target; patient stratification and carefully defined therapeutic windows will be essential for clinical translation.

articles.title: Neutrophil-based drug delivery systems: Platform design, pharmaceutical development, and translational readiness.
articles.abstract: Neutrophils combine rapid recruitment to inflamed tissue with transendothelial migration, phagocytosis, and immunoregulatory activity, making them useful but biologically complex drug carriers. Here, we examine neutrophil-based drug delivery systems (NDDs) through the lens of pharmaceutical development. We distinguish three platform types: intact neutrophils, neutrophil membrane-coated nanoparticles, and neutrophil-derived vesicular systems, the latter encompassing naturally released extracellular vesicles and engineered membrane-derived nanovesicles. Their performance is compared across cargo incorporation and release, preservation of neutrophil function, tissue recruitment, barrier crossing, in vivo persistence, manufacturability, quality control, and safety. Preclinical studies in cancer, inflammatory disease, cardiovascular injury, and central nervous system disorders show that these platforms can exploit inflammatory trafficking, but also reveal substantial variability in cell source, formulation design, dose, and experimental endpoints. Direct comparisons between platform classes are rare, so no platform can yet be considered generally superior. Key development problems include inconsistent loading in living cells, poorly defined release kinetics, short persistence, donor- and source-dependent heterogeneity, uncertain contributions of carrier and payload to efficacy, and limited manufacturing standardization. Genetic modification, responsive release designs, and externally guided cell systems may solve selected problems, but each adds new control and production requirements. Progress toward translation will depend on defining platform-specific critical quality attributes and on testing formulations with comparable pharmaceutical and pharmacological endpoints.

articles.title: Advancing exosome research through artificial intelligence: Advancements and applications.
articles.abstract: Exosomes, secreted by all cell types, range in size from 30 nm to 150 nm and play roles in intercellular communication. Due to their extreme stability, low immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers, including the blood-brain barrier, they are being proposed as excellent candidates for prognosis, disease diagnosis, as biological nanocarriers, and targeted therapies. However, the heterogeneity and complexity of exosomal cargo, nonreproducibility in their isolation and characterization protocols, and lack of standardized analytical pipelines hinder knowledge translation into clinical practice. Recent advances in machine learning and deep learning algorithms of artificial intelligence (AI) have revolutionized every stage of exosome research, from their isolation to characterization and analysis. AI synergism in exosome research enables automated exosome isolation, automated profiling, multimodal data integration, and engineering of exosomes, which facilitate targeted drug delivery, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic cargo prediction. AI integration with multiomics platforms, including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and imaging data, facilitates the development of predictive models capable of improving diagnostic accuracy and accelerating therapeutic discovery. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the synergistic potential of AI and exosome biology in biomedical research. It discusses the biological properties of exosomes, emerging AI methodologies applied to exosome research, recent breakthroughs in AI-assisted biomarker discovery, and its applications. We further examine the challenges associated with data quality, model interpretability, clinical validation, regulatory frameworks, and ethical considerations. Finally, we highlight future perspectives involving foundation models, multimodal biological AI, federated learning, and explainable AI, which collectively have the potential to transform exosome research into a cornerstone of precision medicine. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Artificial intelligence is transforming exosome research by enhancing protocols for their isolation, characterization, thereby assisting biomarker discovery, multiomics integration, and therapeutic engineering. This review provides a comprehensive overview of AI-assisted approaches in exosome research, highlighting recent advances, clinical applications, current challenges, and future opportunities for precision diagnostics and personalized medicine, thereby serving as a valuable resource for researchers across biomedical, computational, and translational disciplines.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence in basic and translational cardiovascular research.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in cardiovascular research where conventional analysis struggles with scale, heterogeneity, and multimodal integration. Its contribution differs across imaging, computational omics, mechanistic simulation, and drug discovery. This narrative review examines substantive applications of machine learning and deep learning while distinguishing them from routine bioinformatics and purely biophysical modeling. We assess independent biological units, validation strategies, and strength of inference in representative studies. Deep-learning imaging systems can provide reproducible quantitative phenotypes, but workflow performance alone does not establish mechanism. In single-cell and spatial studies, clustering, integration, trajectory inference, and network reconstruction generally yield associations or hypotheses unless experimentally supported. Mechanistic interpretation is bounded by the specific effect established through targeted perturbation or rescue with functional testing; lineage tracing and orthogonal readouts provide complementary support, not standalone proof of causation. Hybrid AI-biophysical models may accelerate personalized simulation, whereas heart-on-chip, engineered tissue, and organoid systems without learned components are validation platforms rather than AI methods. In drug discovery, active learning and molecular redesign can prioritize candidates, but predicted reductions in ion-channel liability do not demonstrate biological safety or reduced proarrhythmic risk. Major limitations include pseudoreplication, data leakage, domain shift, batch effects, uncertain labels, few independent hearts, demographic imbalance, incomplete calibration, and limited transfer among animal, iPSC-derived, and adult human systems. AI is most valuable when it produces robust phenotypes or experimentally testable hypotheses within a transparent validation framework, rather than when predictive accuracy is treated as mechanistic evidence.

articles.title: Medicinal plants of the Ukraine: from Prince Volodymyr (10th century) to medicinal Cannabis (2026).
articles.abstract: Ukraine has a unique ethnopharmacological heritage shaped by its exceptional floristic diversity, complex political history, and long-standing cross-cultural interactions with neighbouring regions. This narrative review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of the historical development of herbal medicine in the territory of modern Ukraine from the prehistoric and medieval periods to the early 21st century. This study is the first to integrate historical, ethnobotanical, and normative aspects and offers a comparative analysis of regional and temporal patterns of medicinal plant use, highlighting key stages in the transformation of medicinal plant use from empirical and ritual practices to institutionalised, evidence-based approaches. The analysis incorporates data from chronicles, monastic and church manuscripts, early herbals, pharmacopoeias, and modern scientific literature. Early stages of development, particularly those associated with Kyivan Rus' (11th-13th centuries), are reconstructed mainly based on indirect and retrospective sources, reflecting cultural understanding of treatment rather than systematically recorded medical practices, highlighting the importance of recognising the limitations of these data. Beginning in the 18th and 19th centuries, the development of university medicine, pharmacognosy, and pharmacopoeial regulation ensured increasingly reliable documentation of herbal medicine knowledge. During the Soviet period, extensive standardisation and industrial application of medicinal plants were introduced, and since independence, Ukraine has seen changes such as the creation of a national pharmacopoeia and increasing integration into European regulatory frameworks, including recent legislative changes regarding Cannabis sativa L. Combining historical reconstruction with a critical evaluation of reliability of sources and regional variability, this review demonstrates how Ukrainian herbal medicine has continually adapted to changing cultural, political, and environmental conditions. The study emphasises the value of historical ethnopharmacological knowledge for hypothesis generation and biodiversity conservation, as well as the need for careful interpretation of early sources within modern, scientifically sound paradigms. It lays the basis for more history-centred archival studies to understand these developments in a European and global context.

articles.title: Comparison of bivalirudin and conventional anticoagulation therapy in percutaneous coronary intervention: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) necessitates efficient periprocedural anticoagulation. Although traditional heparin-based protocols have been the norm, apprehensions about bleeding risk and variable responses remain. Bivalirudin, a direct thrombin inhibitor, presents a potential alternative; nonetheless, its relative efficacy and safety compared to heparin remain ambiguous due to inconsistent findings from previous trials and meta-analyses. This systematic review and meta-analysis seeks to offer a modern synthesis comparing bivalirudin with traditional anticoagulation in patients having percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). MATERIALS AND METHODS: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) and the Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR) standards. A thorough search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from inception to 15 December 2025, identified randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing bivalirudin versus heparin-based regimens (with or without glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors) in adult patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). The primary outcomes comprised primary endpoint(death, MI or major bleeding), all-cause mortality(death), myocardial infarction (MI), stent thrombosis, revascularisation, significant bleeding and Stroke at 30 days. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias evaluation. The statistical analysis was conducted using the random or fixed effect model in Review Manager v5.3, and subgroup analyses were performed according to the publication year (before 2010 and after 2010), the type of STEMI, and whether Glycoprotein IIbIIIa was combined.The certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE. RESULTS: Bivalirudin significantly reduced the primary endpoint (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.76-0.98, P < 0.00001, I2 = 76%) and major bleeding (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.46-0.79, P < 0.00001, I2 = 83%). All-cause mortality (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80-1.05, P = 0.23), MI, stent thrombosis, revascularization, and stroke did not differ significantly. The bleeding advantage of the group receiving heparin combined with GPI was the most significant (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.45-0.59), while this benefit in the heparin monotherapy group was less pronounced (P = 0.05). The post-2010 subgroup showed a diminished but persistent bleeding benefit (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.42-0.87). Certainty of evidence was high for bleeding, moderate for the primary endpoint and death, and low for ischemic outcomes. CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing PCI, bivalirudin is associated with a significant reduction in the primary composite endpoint and major bleeding compared with heparin, but this finding is primarily driven by trials where heparin was combined with planned GPI. Against heparin monotherapy, the bleeding benefit is attenuated and not statistically robust. The bleeding benefit, though attenuated, persists in contemporary practice. All-cause mortality was not significantly reduced, and previous mortality claims should be interpreted cautiously. The choice of anticoagulant should be individualised based on bleeding risk, ischemic risk, access site, and bivalirudin infusion protocol. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO (CRD420261289024).

articles.title: Translational pharmacology of (+)-terrein: from biological activity to oral and periodontal therapeutic development.
articles.abstract: Previous terrein reviews have emphasized its isolation, synthesis, production, and broad biological activities. Among the prior reviews identified in the literature, no oral/dental indication-specific critical appraisal was found that integrated chemical comparability, evidence directness, exposure, target engagement, formulation, safety, and reproducibility. The present review therefore critically appraised (+)-terrein as a focused case study in oral translational pharmacology and as a model for examining natural-product drug-development bottlenecks. Terrein-specific literature searches were updated through 14 September 2026 in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection. The three database searches identified 411 records; after removal of 160 duplicates, 251 unique records remained. Application of predefined eligibility criteria yielded 61 original studies forming the qualitative evidence base, of which 27 underwent structured in-depth appraisal using explicit author-defined criteria. Recurrent biological activity was reported across multiple experimental contexts and by groups without author overlap with the principal oral/skeletal research network, whereas the integrated oral/skeletal evidence sequence remains concentrated within an overlapping collaborative network. Early studies employed fungus-isolated, racemic, or incompletely comparable preparations, whereas later periodontal and skeletal studies predominantly used synthetic (+)-terrein. Biochemical inhibition of the 20S proteasome has been reported at relatively high concentrations; however, no dominant molecular target has been pharmacologically validated at exposure levels corresponding to the key periodontal cellular models. Formal parent-compound pharmacokinetics, periodontal tissue-exposure data, and a clinically relevant oral/periodontal formulation also remain unavailable. A tumor-targeted nanocarrier study provides proof-of-concept for formulation but does not establish oral exposure or periodontal delivery. Among the indications examined, periodontitis provides the most integrated preclinical sequence, linking responses in human gingival fibroblasts, osteoclast inhibition, and a disease-specific mouse model. In that model, the reduction in micro-CT-assessed alveolar bone resorption did not reach statistical significance, despite significant osteoclast- and TNF-α-related effects; moreover, dosing represented systemic preventive/early intervention rather than local treatment of established disease. Further development therefore requires chemical standardization, exposure-response characterization, orthogonal target validation, an oral/periodontal formulation, indication-specific safety assessment, and replication of the periodontal findings by an independent laboratory. Collectively, the available evidence supports (+)-terrein as an experimental pharmacological and drug-development scaffold rather than as a clinically validated therapy.

articles.title: Therapeutic potential of eucommia in chronic metabolic diseases: phytochemical basis, pharmacological actions, and molecular mechanisms.
articles.abstract: Chronic metabolic diseases, mainly including obesity, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, are characterized by disorders of glucose and lipid metabolism, abnormal energy homeostasis, chronic low-grade inflammation, and multi-organ dysfunction. With the increasing global burden of these diseases, natural medicines and medicine-food homology resources with potential metabolic regulatory properties have attracted growing attention, although their long-term efficacy and safety require further investigation. Eucommia ulmoides Oliver (Eucommiaceae), hereafter referred to as Eucommia, is a traditional tonic herb in China and has long been used to tonify the liver and kidney and strengthen bones and muscles. Its medicinal bark (Eucommia Cortex), leaves (Eucommia Folium), flowers, and seeds contain diverse bioactive constituents, including iridoids, phenolic acids, flavonoids, lignans, terpenoids, and polysaccharides. Preclinical studies suggest that Eucommia and its bioactive constituents may exert beneficial effects on metabolic abnormalities through several potential mechanisms, including the regulation of fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis, insulin resistance, gut microbiota and microbial metabolites, bile acid metabolism, oxidative stress, inflammation, and autophagy, as well as potential protective effects on metabolism-related organs. However, these findings require further validation in human studies. This narrative review summarizes the phytochemical basis, reported pharmacological activities, and proposed molecular mechanisms of Eucommia in chronic metabolic diseases, and discusses the potential of its Folium as a renewable complementary resource, while critically considering the limitations of current evidence regarding clinical efficacy, long-term safety, and environmental and economic sustainability.

articles.title: Drug repurposing and treatment optimisation in oncology: regulatory challenges and policy priorities.
articles.abstract: Drug repurposing and treatment optimisation are increasingly important strategies to improve cancer outcomes by making better use of existing therapies. Drug repurposing involves identifying new clinical indications for approved or abandoned medicines, while treatment optimisation focuses on refining how established therapies are used within their licensed indications, for example, through dose, duration, or sequencing modifications. Although both approaches aim to maximise patient benefit and are supported by extensive clinical experience, they face distinct and shared regulatory challenges. We examine why current regulatory and legislative frameworks remain poorly aligned with the objectives, risk profiles, and evidentiary needs of drug repurposing and treatment optimisation studies. Drawing on illustrative case studies in oncology, including aspirin and metformin repurposing, immunotherapy optimisation, and regulatory initiatives such as Project Optimus, we demonstrate how regulatory systems designed primarily for de novo drug development create disproportionate burdens, delay evidence generation, and impede translation into routine clinical practice. The heterogeneity of evidence across prevention and treatment settings, the absence of clear licensing pathways for off-patent medicines, and the limited integration of optimisation into post-authorisation management are recurring themes. This review highlights how regulatory bottlenecks arise across the trial life cycle and how diverse treatment optimisation study designs could better address patient-centred outcomes. We propose that proportionate regulatory frameworks encompassing marketing authorisation, post-authorisation evidence generation, and reimbursement mechanisms are necessary to enable the efficient evaluation, regulatory approval, and sustainable implementation of repurposed and treatment-optimised therapies. Aligning regulation with real-world cancer care requires coordinated action from regulators, policymakers, academia, industry and clinicians to ensure that established medicines are not only approved, but used optimally to deliver meaningful, evidence-based benefit.

articles.title: Unraveling the molecular basis of ADC-related interstitial lung disease: from structural determinants to pathogenic pathways and mitigation strategies.
articles.abstract: Despite being a revolutionary class of precision oncology therapeutics, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) face growing restrictions on clinical application due to one of their most significant and life-threatening side effects-interstitial lung disease (ILD). The incidence of ADC-related ILD (ADC-ILD) exhibits marked heterogeneity across agents (less than 1% to more than 15%), indicating that this toxicity is not a general class effect, but rather fundamentally linked to the molecular structure of individual ADC molecules. This review synthesizes the association of structural elements of ADCs (linker chemistry, properties of payload, drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR), and target selection) with the risk of ILD, based on clinical data and insights into the mechanism. We propose a multidimensional risk model, informed primarily by trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) mechanistic studies, wherein pulmonary toxicity may arise from the convergence of three structural liabilities: cleavable linkers, high DAR, and membrane-permeable payloads.
